lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- A Tuesday in the Practice
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Veridiana Sterman Petrilli | Lesson 11 -- A Tuesday in the Practice

listenings.text: I run a small dental practice in Miami, and people always ask me what a normal day looks like. So here is a normal Tuesday. I get up at six, I walk the dog, and I am at the practice by seven thirty. We open at eight. Most of my Tuesday patients come in for a check-up or a cleaning, so the morning moves fast. I usually stop for lunch at twelve thirty, and I eat at my desk, which my husband says is a terrible habit. In the afternoon I see the more complicated cases, and I finish at five. That is a normal Tuesday. This month is not normal. We are redoing the waiting room, so right now we are seeing patients in two small rooms upstairs, and everything takes a little longer. One of my hygienists is on maternity leave, so I am taking over some of her cleanings myself. And because of all that, I am not eating at my desk these days. I am not eating lunch at all, and my husband is not happy about that either.

I coordinate the English program at a bilingual school, and every March parents ask me the same question: what does my child actually do in English all week? Here is the short answer. The younger children have English every morning, from eight to eleven. They read together on Mondays and Wednesdays, they do science in English on Tuesdays, and on Fridays each child presents something to the class. The older students have fewer hours, but their classes are harder, and they write a short text every week. That is the normal routine. This term, though, we are trying something new. We are sending a short reading home every Thursday, with three questions, and we are asking parents to read it with their children. You do not need perfect English for this. Most parents are reading in English for the first time in years, and the children love correcting them. So if your daughter is laughing at your pronunciation, the program is working.
